title: AAO Non-Precedent Decision — Application for T Nonimmigrant Status (2025-11-13)
text:
U.S. Citizenship Non-Precedent Decision of the
and Immigration Administrative Appeals Office
Services
In Re: 39418066 Date: NOV. 13, 2025
Appeal of Service Center Operations (SCOPS) Decision
Form 1-914, Application for T Nonimmigrant Status
The Applicant seeks T-1 nonimmigrant classification as a victim of human trafficking under sections
101(a)(15)(T) and 214(0) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (the Act), 8 U.S.C. sections
1101(a)(l5)(T) and 1184(0).
Service Center Operations (SCOPS) denied the application, concluding that the Applicant did not
submit a valid application or supporting documents due to signature deficiencies. The matter is now
before us on appeal pursuant to 8 C.F.R. § 103.3.
The Applicant bears the burden ofproof to demonstrate eligibility by a preponderance ofthe evidence.
Matter oJChawathe, 25 l&N Dec. 369, 375-76 (AAO 2010). We review the questions in this matter
de novo. Matter of Christa's, Inc. , 26 I&N Dec. 537,537 n.2 (AAO 2015). Upon de novo review,
we will dismiss the appeal.
After receiving the Applicant's Form 1-914, Application for T Nonimmigrant Status (T application),
SCOPS issued a notice of intent to deny (NOID) informing the Applicant that the T application did
not appear to be a photocopy of a document personally signed by the Applicant and therefore did not
conform to signature requirements. In the decision denying the application, SCOPS noted that the
appearance of the Applicant's signature was exactly the same on multiple documents, which was the
functional equivalent of a stamp. The Applicant's NOID response included a second application form,
but did not include the original or copy of the T application the Applicant originally submitted. The
Applicant had therefore not shown that she personally signed the T application prior to filing.
On appeal, the Applicant asserts that she properly submitted her original application because the
documents she submitted included an electronically reproduced copy of her original handwritten
signature. She contends that guidance provided by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
(USCIS) indicates that signatures are considered valid even if the original signature on the document
is a "photocopied, scanned, faxed, or similarly reproduced" copy ofthe original handwritten signature.
Moreover, the Applicant states that the NOID response cured the deficiencies in the original
application. Furthermore, she argues that SCOPS' denial of the application for the signature
deficiencies stems from an overly formalistic, technical interpretation of the regulations and raises due
process concerns for a vulnerable individual who should benefit from a victim-centered approach and

whose application was pending for over a year. The Applicant requests that we exercise discretion to
accept the application for these reasons.
Upon de novo review, the Applicant has not overcome the reasons for the denial of the T application.
The Applicant's signature appears to have been copied and pasted or created by a stamp or similar
device for use on multiple documents. This is not acceptable as a valid signature because the
regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(a)(2) specifies that non-electronic applications require "handwritten"
signatures, which include the instant application. Applicants are required to sign their benefit requests.
Id.
We discern no distinction between a digitally "cut and paste" signature and the simulated signatures
created by word processor, stamp, auto-pen, or similar device, as they all may be used to replicate a
person's signature without their direct involvement in the act of signing. Each format may be created
or applied by someone other than the signatory, in violation of 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(a)(2). In this case,
the signature is invalid because it does not signify the purported signatory knows the contents of the
request and supporting documents submitted on their behalf: that they have reviewed and approved of
the information therein, and that they have certified the truth and correctness of the request under
penalty of perjury. See Form 1-914, Part 6.
The probative force of a benefit request subscribed under penalty of perjury derives from the actual
signature of the applicant or petitioner. 28 U.S.C. § 1746 (requiring the signature of the declarant);
see also US. v. Bueno-Vargas, 383 F.3d 1104, 1111 (9th Cir. 2004) ("We conclude that signing a
statement under penalty of perjury satisfies the standard for an oath or affirmation, as it is a signal that
the declarant understands the legal significance of the declarant's statements and the potential for
punishment if the declarant lies."). By requiring an applicant or petitioner to verify the truth of the
benefit request, the submitted evidence, and the related claims by personally reviewing and signing
the immigration form under penalty ofperjury, USCIS aims to ensure the accuracy ofthe information.
Only the applicant or petitioner can attest to the truth of these matters. When a USCIS form is not
signed by the applicant or petitioner to attest to its veracity, the evidentiary basis for the application
or petition and supporting evidence no longer exists.
Additionally, the signature requirement safeguards the protections accorded an applicant or petitioner
under 8 U.S.C. § 1367 ("Penalties for disclosure of information"), as required in the current
matter. See also 8 C.F.R. § 214.216 (setting forth restrictions on the use and disclosure ofinformation
relating to T applicants). The signature on a T application authorizes the release of protected privacy
information in limited circumstances that, if erroneous, could endanger the applicant and violate
privacy laws. See 8 C.F.R. § 103.2(b)(16) ("Inspection of evidence"); see also Form 1-914, Part 6.
The Applicant further asserts that the filing is consistent with the intent of regulations, yet she does
not claim, nor has she demonstrated, that she personally signed the documents initially submitted with
the T application. The Applicant cannot cure this by later submitting an additional application
associated with the same filing. An applicant may not make material changes to an application that
has already been filed in an effort to make a deficient application conform to USCIS requirements.
Matter ofIzummi, 22 I&N Dec. 169, 175 (Assoc. Comm'r 1998).
2

Although we acknowledge the difficulties the Applicant claims she will face as a result of the adverse
finding in her case here, we lack the authority to waive or disregard any of the Act's requirements, as
implemented by regulation. See United States v. Nixon, 418 U.S. 683,695 (1974) (providing that "[s]o
long as this regulation is extant it has the force oflaw"). Moreover, SCOPS' decision was procedurally
appropriate despite the Applicant's concern that the application was first accepted and later denied.
The review and analysis of a questionable signature is an adjudication itself and it is appropriate to
deny a benefit request when it is not properly signed under penalty of perjury.
In conclusion, the Applicant has not overcome the reasons for the denial on appeal and the application
will remain denied. Furthermore, this decision is without prejudice to any application the Applicant
may wish to file in the future.
ORDER: The appeal is dismissed.
NOTICE: This constitutes the final decision in this matter. The filing of a motion will not postpone the
effect of the decision. 8 C.F.R. § 103.S(a)(l)(iv). Aliens who are not lawfully present, or who are
otherwise inadmissible or deportable, may be subject to the commencement of removal proceedings
under section 240 of the Act through the issuance of a Form I-862, Notice to Appear. Those proceedings
may result in their removal from the United States and possible ineligibility for future visas or other
immigration benefits.
